title: Judaism: repair
hookLine: many Jews speak of repairing the world, a phrase with old mystical and modern meanings

lines: THE WORLD THAT FEELS TOO BIG.
cards: Somewhere in your home there's a thing that's been broken for months. A drawer that sticks. A lamp with a loose switch.
A shirt missing one button, folded at the bottom of the pile. You walk past it every day. It's too small to matter, and somehow too annoying to fix.
Now zoom out. The street has its broken things too. So does the town, the country, the whole world, and all of it can feel far too big for one person.
Jewish tradition has a phrase that sits right between the button and the world. Today: tikkun olam.

teach.b: Tikkun means repair, or setting right. Olam means world. Repairing the world.
Today many Jews use the phrase for acts of justice and kindness: feeding people, protecting the vulnerable, caring for the earth. But the phrase has lived several lives. The first life is legal.

teach.h: FOR THE GOOD ORDER OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: In the Mishnah, the rabbis made certain adjustments to the law, about divorce documents and freeing captives, and gave their reason as for the repair of the world, meaning to keep society in good working order.
The second life is in prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of Jewish services, hopes for a day when the world will be set right under the kingship of God. The third life is mystical.
In the sixteenth century, in the hill town of Safed, the teacher Isaac Luria told a remarkable story.
At creation, divine light was poured into vessels too fragile to hold it, and they shattered.

teach.h: NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT YOURS TO QUIT.
teach.b: Sparks of holiness fell and scattered into everything. Every good deed, every blessing, every commandment kept, lifts a spark back up and helps mend what broke.

In modern times the phrase grew wider again, and many Jewish groups made it a banner for social action. Jews themselves debate how the old and new meanings fit together, and that debate is part of the story.
And Pirkei Avot keeps a saying from Rabbi Tarfon: it isn't your job to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either.

how: Many Jewish communities and families organize acts of service, charity and advocacy under the name tikkun olam; some also connect everyday commandments and blessings to Isaac Luria's idea of lifting sparks.

the Jewish law of charity given to the poor
repairing the world, through justice and holy acts

p: adjusting the law for the world's good order

s: tikkun olam is a modern slogan with no older history
it appears in the Mishnah, in the Aleinu prayer, and in Lurianic mysticism.
in Luria's picture, good deeds lift scattered sparks
vessels shattered at creation, and each good act helps gather the light back.

games.q: the world's broken things feel far too big for you. what does Rabbi Tarfon's saying suggest?
o: fix everything, or it doesn't count.
do your part, even if you can't finish.
games.why: Pirkei Avot keeps his saying: the work isn't yours to finish, but you aren't free to walk away from it.

practice: Let one broken thing come to mind: the sticking drawer, the loose button, a message you owe someone, a small promise that cracked. Choose one you could mend, and picture your hands doing it, start to finish.
Not the world, just one spark.

wordCard.voice: Tikkun olam. Repairing the world: a legal phrase, a line of prayer, a mystical picture of gathering sparks, and a call to justice. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: repair. One spark lifted is one small corner of the world mended. See you tomorrow.
